utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, this is the image at 13.37 on the 4th of February, 1994, which presents the shell, which is half or partly under the ground, and there is -- with the part above it and a map with a compass on it. Thank you very much for this answer. I believe we can move a little bit more forward. [In English] Just a little bit, high speed. Now slow down, please. Slow down, please. No, not yet, go ahead. Go ahead, high speed, please. Stop here. Okay, okay, okay. Now switch to French.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what do we see here above the compass?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Above it we see the point of impact. That is where the projectile landed. And one sees the crater and the stabiliser which is lodged in the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And same question, this is the state in which you found this object when you arrived at the scene, is it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so, that is the state in which we found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [In English] Can we now go with the video, please. Normal speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [In English] Okay, forward high speed, please. This is not for the booth, but for the Chamber and us, that we are about to arrive, yes, here we are. We're again at Markale. We are again at Markale for the transcript, and I say when we have to stop. It is a place where we shall see marks on the ground. [In English] Sorry, stop here and go back a little bit, please. Go back a little bit. Yeah, okay. Stop here. Stop here, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this is once again the place which we could see a moment ago, a while ago. And I'd like you to compare this image with that which we saw a while ago where on both occasions, we could see the fins free, or at least visible in the crater. Can one see here the fins in the crater, the tail-fins in the crater?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On this one, you cannot see the tail-fins, or rather in this videorecording you cannot see them because they were covered with the soil, with the dirt which is beneath the asphalt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who removed this soil around?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cleared this area here, and I tried -- rather, I wanted to have a look at the crater to see if there were parts of the firing pin, and then I realised that the tail-fins of the projectiles were there, and I stopped what I was doing pending the arrival of the UN, as I've already said three or four times before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, with regard to this point of impact, what is the distance between this point of impact and the building which is right above it, roughly towards north?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said before that it was about 3 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what you did not say was how tall was the building which was some 3 metres away?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was not asked that question. What I can say is that it is about 5 metres, 4 or 5 metres tall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, and near to the point of impact, wasn't there a building which had six, maybe seven floors?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that building is to the side of the market. It is -- it has six floors, and it is to the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to proceed with the tape, please. [In English] Continue with the video, please. High speed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [In English] Stop here. Back. Back a little bit. Go back a little bit. Stop here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, are we talking about this building here?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This street is on Mula Mustafe, formally Marsal Tito Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [In English] Play the videotape, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [In English] Okay, sorry, go forward. High speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go back, please. Go back. [In English] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Stop here, please. Stop here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what we have here, Witness, can you confirm to us that when the UNPROFOR forces arrived that it was they who got rid of the debris which was above the tail-fins. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have now finished with this tape. I simply have another exhibit to show -- another document to show the witness, but a document this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. You indicated that you would need approximately half an hour. If you would be perhaps more efficient and just in order to give some guidance, perhaps to both parties, a lot of questions are about where a tunnel was situated. And of course I waited to see whether the importance of the situation of the -- the exact location of the tunnel was, but I found it was just to find out where it was. I really wonder whether the parties could, for example, not compromise on where this tunnel was. Why do we have to spend time in this court on where the tunnel was? Apart from who was guarding it, whoever used it, but the mere location of the tunnel, I think it's not easy to change the location of a tunnel. And as far as I know, there's a lot of documentation about that. So I wonder why we have to ask witnesses, perhaps one witness, perhaps more witnesses, on where exactly a tunnel was located where there could hardly at least as far as my knowledge goes at this moment on where this tunnel was. But I'm just indicating how we can speed up, how we can use our time more efficiently. Please proceed, but keep this in mind, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, because you took 50 minutes for what you said would take approximately half an hour. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite. I thought it was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. important for the Chamber to know how far from it was the incident at Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, don't start a debate again. Of course, if you'd like to know the distance between the incident and the beginning of the tunnel, apart from that, these are facts you could easily compromise upon and the parties did not. So if you want us to be informed about these details, try the most efficient way of achieving it. I'm looking to both parties. I mean, both the incident of Dobrinja could, unless -- but I didn't hear it until now -- could be easily demonstrated also in other ways, and you could easily compromise. It's my view. If you say there's any dispute about the exact location of the incident, if there's any dispute about the entrance of the tunnel, please spend as much time as you want on it. But if there's in dispute about that, please compromise on these kind of issues. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to make those compromises. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, we will show you a piece which is Document D65. And I'm going to read a passage from it, but first of all, I'm going to ask for it to be handed out by Mr. Usher, please. Now, Witness, in the meantime could I ask you if you read English?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have before you a document. For the transcript, it is a United Nations document from the Security Council. And I will simply read to you the very last sentence: "The conclusions that the Commission of Experts reached," and the last sentence, I'm quoting the very last sentence, and I believe that the interpreters have it on the screen: "...The mortar bomb in question could therefore have been fired by either side." End of quotation. Now, Witness, were you ever informed of the existence of such a correspondence dated the 16th of February, 1994, and signed by Mr. Boutros Boutros Ghali who was at the time the Secretary-General?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not receive this document, and it is not within my competence to receive it since I am just someone who was carrying out tasks and it is up to the Prosecutor and other authorities who were supposed to be given or receive this correspondence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now Mr. President, to save time, we have another document that we will also produce under the number of D66, which is, in fact -- but we will show in a minute. We will change the number, correct the number, which is the same source of the document, which is the annex 6 to the final expert report for the day of the 5th of February, 1994, which also gives the results of the Commission of Experts. And we will also show it and tender, but I don't think that it is actually necessary to show it to the witness since the witness cannot read English. And this document is originating from the UN and is to do with the correspondence of the 16th of February, 1994. So if you do not ask me to show it, I won't. But I would tender it since the origin of the document is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tender as proof of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the existence, Mr. President, of a Commission, an ad hoc Commission, which was established at the time, and of the results that this Commission reached, and the conclusion being that the both parties could have fired this mortar shell, if there was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The objection, which is a mild objection if I may put it that way, to what my friend is doing is because of the procedure because he is proposing to tender a document through a witness who knows nothing about it. Those documents were given to the Defence by the Prosecution. If the Court would have a look at the letter that we have sent in respect of those documents, those are part of the Prosecution case, and the Prosecution expects to tender those documents through members of that same Commission. So this witness can't speak to it. There are forthcoming witnesses who created those documents who are going to be called by the Prosecution, and the documents are a part of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So as a matter of fact, what we are doing now is to establish that these documents do exist. Let's just assume that these are not forgeries and that these are copies of real United Nations documents. Wouldn't it be -- at least that's what I assume the parties were to present us with any documents which have the look of a United Nations document. I do understand that Mr. Stamp says these documents will be tendered by us soon, and especially the last part of your -- the last document you intended to enter you said we don't have to show to the witness because he can't read any English. So I would say wouldn't it be better, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that if there's no direct relationship with this witness, although, of course, there is a direct relationship of these documents with the incident we are dealing with at this moment, that perhaps you first wait and see that these documents are tendered as a -- in direct relation with the testimony of a witness. And if the Prosecution would forget any document, then of course we would have to think about introducing documentary evidence without any witness. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please give your view on this --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Simply this: It seems useful that we tender these -- that we show these documents to the witness so that I can ask him questions on the simple fact if he has ever seen these documents, if he has ever seen them. And I believe it is important because we are talking about his knowledge about this Commission. And we see that he was never interested in the results of the Commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you have asked, I noticed, five times approximately on whether any result of a UN investigation became known to the department of the witness, to the witness himself, whether they ever asked for it. Okay, that's clear. If you just want to establish that even this document and this conclusion of this Committee ever became known, I'd rather say that if we just, for the transcript, say that Document S1994-182, an official United Nations document, Security Council, in its original version, English, has been put to the witness, that a part has been translated to him, and that he has testified that he was not aware of the existence of the document or of this conclusion, would that be good enough to the time being as part of his testimony, especially since we can expect that this document will be tendered in a later stage by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I am afraid that I will have to give you a negative answer and I am very sorry about it. First of all, we don't know at all that the Prosecution will tender these documents, first of all. We could see that the Prosecution changed its mind very often. And on the other hand, it is very important for the Defence to know if the person who was in charge of this investigation has ever seen these documents. That's why we want to show them. That's a fundamental question, yes or no. I can explain why it is fundamental.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For several reasons, but being one of them that the Prosecution intends to tender these documents anyhow. If they are admitted in evidence it means that we can take it into consideration while making out deliberations, so they can be admitted in evidence. So the objection is denied. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we proceed, could I ask that the second document be circulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. It has to be circulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was obviously about to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document has been returned to the Defence so that they can present it in an orderly manner. Perhaps we'll wait until they have prepared for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we put the first page so that we can be certain of what we have here. The first page is a cover page, simply so that we don't have any problems. And the document consists of three pages, and it is -- it relates to the UNPROFOR dated 5th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, what pages? I see one cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What pages apart from the cover page are part of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have pages 781, 82, 83 that you see before you. But I simply gave the cover page as well because I wanted to avoid any problems from the side of the Prosecution as to the origin of the document. And the cover page is only indicative of the source, of the origin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you're tendering a document with some pages attached to each other, other pages loose. Would you please present us in an orderly manner, that means first page first, attached to the second or the third or whatever other page you'd like to use, and present it in this way. Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well, Mr. President. The reason for what you have is that at the time when we made the photocopies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I'm not that interested in the reasons, although I have a full understanding that you might have faced difficulties. What I'm interested in is to receive orderly copies of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will have as soon as the photocopy machine starts functioning. It is out of order, and the Defence can do nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, how many pages can we -- the whole report?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. There are three pages that I told you about, 781, 782, and 783.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you need, as a matter of fact, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is scissors to separate page 782 from 783. Then you need a stapler in order to connect the front page to page 781 as the first, 782 as the second, and 783 as the third, and as far as I can see, you're not in need of any photocopying facilities for doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Be glad to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that will for the time, that's for the document tendered. Please proceed. We'll help ourselves with the disorderly copies. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before my friend proceeds, may I just state for the record, I did make an error when I said the Prosecution intended to tender this document. I made that statement having not seen the document because my friend said he was producing the report of the United Nations' team of experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I understood as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is not the report of the United Nations' team of experts. When I indicated to the Court that that report was part of our case, I was not referring to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that you are now presenting us with annex 6 to the report of the Committee of Experts usually called the Cousico [phoen], or the Commission D'experts, which of course is a different committee. But at least it has been clarified that this will not be tendered by the Prosecution. Please then proceed, having established that this is not experts -- it's the same committee as the other document was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what I said was that in these documents, there were, as well as in the letter that we saw a moment ago, there were conclusions of experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have before you certain documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you have before you -- you have a before you a document. Have you ever seen such a document in the past?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never seen such a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If the document could be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, Mr. Stamp asked whether it could be put on the ELMO. We have a couple of pages in front of us. Would, first of all, the front page which will not be tendered into evidence, will that be returned to the Defence. Would you then, please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you are putting questions to the witness concerning this document, indicate clearly which page you're referring to or to all three pages, and have page 781 at this moment on the ELMO. Mr. Usher, could you please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I treated this document as a whole, because it is a whole. But I could see page by page, I could show him whether he's seen one page, second page, third page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you see this page or a document of this kind?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have before you 782, after you have seen 781. Have you seen a page like this, or any similar page previously?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never seen. I did not have opportunity to see such a document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to quote -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Leave it, Mr. Usher. Leave it as it was. I'm going to quote. You can stop here. I can quote what is on the ELMO, I'm going to read the second sentence, which is relating to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness says he has never seen the documents. He does not know the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But what I understand Mr. Piletta-Zanin wants is to confront the witness with the findings of some other body.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. As it pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I don't know what question will be attached to it. But it does not seem to be inadmissible. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to quote the second sentence of the first paragraph that we can read on the top of the page. And the grammatical subject being the UNPROFOR, since some of the words are hidden by the margin, I'm going to guess. So I'm going to start with "but." "But that it had not been possible to determine the exact origin of the launch and noted that Bosnian Serb and BiH forces had positions close to other northeast of the city." That is end of quote. Now, Witness, and this is my very last question: You have never heard of this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Besic, you have been asked questions by the Defence. I'll first ask the Prosecution whether there's any need to re-examine Mr. Besic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a couple questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. Re-examined by Mr. Stamp:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were just shown by my friend a tape including incidents of the 4th of February, 1994, a tape recording, an investigation of the incident of the 4th of February, 1994, in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The extracts you were shown are from the tape which you brought to this Tribunal last week?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the original tape which is the only one that the police -- the police is the only one that has that. No one else has that tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First Judge Nieto-Navia has some questions for you. Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I would like you to clarify for me and for the Chamber, from which direction came the shell which exploded in the market, cardinal points, I mean north, south, east, west, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Northeast, from the northeast side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Northeast. According to your knowledge, in that part of the -- not of the city but of the outskirts of the city -- were the Serb army and the BH army close to each other?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that -- on that side was -- were the confrontation lines of the BH army and -- of the BH army members and of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Elmahdi also has a question for you. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to ask you to inform me on the subject of some details that I would like to know more about, please. The first detail is to do with what you said. If I remember well, you said that you waited -- and I'm talking about the incident in the Markale market, at the marketplace in Markale -- you said that you waited for the arrival of the UNPROFOR. Was that normal, or rather why did you wait? Did they inform you that they were coming? Did you know that they were going to come? Did they tell you to wait for them so that they would carry out the investigation? Could you please give me the answer on this point.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when we arrived to the -- at the site of the incident together with our colleagues, and five minutes later the Prosecutor and the judge arrived. We started to carry out the investigation at the moment when the judge gave his permission to carry out the investigation, we started the work. We did not know that the UNPROFOR members would arrive, but they did arrive after 15 minutes, as I said in my testimony. At the time we were carrying out the investigation until the UNPROFOR arrived, the investigation team was carrying out the investigation. When the UNPROFOR arrived, they simply joined the investigation. When the UN members arrived, we continued the teamwork. We showed them the crater. We showed them where the stabiliser was, and on the videotape, it is possible to see that they did it. It happened in cases where there were a large number of victims that UNPROFOR members would come to see what happened. In the case of Dobrinja, the UNPROFOR members did not attend our investigation. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. I mean, no. You said -- yes, I mean, you, that is, your investigating team "clear the crater, because the stabiliser is in it." So my question is, I'd like you to tell me if it was a normal procedure, was it a part of your job, of your task, with the -- to turn over the work to the UNPROFOR, or was it that they wanted to help? I'd simply like you to tell me, because you said that you told them, you asked them or requested from them to perform a part of what is your chief job?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, we performed our investigation, and we always did it independently of UNPROFOR members. This time we conducted our investigation normally, but when the UN members arrived, we wanted them to do their job to see what it was all about and what the crater was like and what was the whole site like, in order to avoid any misunderstandings, any dilemmas, or any ideas about anything else. And that is why. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you. I shall move to another question. You said that you took the photograph, that you took photographs of the market, and there was a building which was used by the police or the army. And you said that -- that it was a kind of a store, that it made clothes, uniforms for the military.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say -- I didn't say it was a storage. I said it was a store, that is, it was a building which had shops on the ground floor. Right now, it is just a store, but before the war, it was selling uniforms, military uniforms and police -- or rather, some part of the gear was also sold there. That is different types of protective clothing for firemen, for forest rangers, all kinds of protective clothing for the -- JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But at the time of the incident, was it still being used as such?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It didn't work, because there was no electricity, they had no fabrics to use. So apart from the stock that they had, and then from those stocks they would sell from time to time, and naturally the civilian clothes because there were no more uniform or police or army uniforms. When I mentioned army clothes, it is those uniforms which were made by the previous army, that is, the Yugoslav People's Army. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Right. Thank you, and my very last question, perhaps it will sound naive, but I'm not an expert. There are -- is there some writing on this stabiliser? That is, are there some codes or some marks or some figures? On the basis of figures that you see or numbers that you see there, can you determine the origin or production series, or is there the number of the series or whatever? How did you identify the make of this -- of the shell or the stabiliser? Or is it impossible? Usually one can trace a weapon because it has a number, and then this number is effaced occasionally to prevent the tracing of this weapon. Did you have any indications of that nature?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on this part of the stabiliser, there are some letters, and there are some numbers. In one it says MM-74, and in the other one it says KB 87-01. "KB" is in Cyrillic letters, and the first two letters are KB -- KV and mean Krusik Valjevo. The year is 87, month 01. So January. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And where is the factory, where is that factory? Could you identify that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is a place called Valjevo in Serbia, and I presume the name of the factory is Krusik, in Valjevo JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Right. I didn't quite follow. You said KB. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would be how it would read in Latin alphabet, but B Latin alphabet is a V in Cyrillic alphabet, so it stands for V. So this KV in Cyrillic letters mean Krusik Valjevo. The year of production, 87, the month of production, January. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Besic, since I've no further questions for you, this ends the examination of you as a witness here. It has been a bit tumultuous perhaps now and then, but as you may have noticed, that apart from the information you have given in response to the questions of the Prosecution and the Defence and of the Judges, there were some other issues we had to deal with as well. Mr. Besic, you may be aware that it's important for this Chamber and for this Tribunal to hear the testimony of witnesses who have been present during those days at the events which are the subject of our cases. And therefore, we are very grateful that the witnesses come and testify in this Court. So this thanks, I'd like also to express in respect of you. We know it's a long way; we know it might not always be easy to come to The Hague and to testify. I wish you a good journey home. And once again thank you for coming and testifying. Mr. Usher, would you please lead then, Mr. Besic, who is now excused out of this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break now, but before we go into the break, we'll first have to deal with the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as the exhibits are concerned, documents might not be that much of a problem. Tapes might be a great problem. I'd like to invite the parties over the next 20 minutes to find out which tape of the three or four we have been talking about, that's 2279, 2279A, and there was even a 2279B prepared, as far as I understand, and the V000-3822 which tape contains all of the passages shown to this Chamber and to agree upon tendering that tape as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you are placing before the Defence an impossible objective. We cannot know which one contains everything, because we need to compare them with all the other tapes. It is much more complicated than to take scissors and cut an exhibit. I believe it is up to the Prosecution to tell us if this or that piece of evidence contains this or that fragment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I invited the parties to see whether they could agree upon it. If not, then we'll hear about it and then we'll take a decision. I'd like to make one additional remark: If I sometimes in very gentle words give you a reprimand, I'm not amused by hearing the words I used in reprimanding you to be repeated again and again by yourself as a toy -- a word toy with which you'd like to play in this courtroom. We'll adjourn until 5 minutes after 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could we perhaps please first start with the easy part, the documents. Could you guide us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2262, photo documentation, 14 pages in B/C/S; P2262.1, English translation. P2309, a report bearing ERN number 0026-8351, report of 5 February, 1994, in B/C/S; P2309.1, English translation. P2247, photo documentation bearing ERN number 0026-8244. P2247.1, English translation. D60, document bearing ERN number 0026-8397. D61, document bearing ERN number 0026-8398. D62, report on the forensic on-site investigation bearing ERN number 0026-8234; D62.1, English translation. D63, a sketch of the stabiliser. D65, a letter of United Nations Security Council dated 15 February, 1994. D66, three pages of a report bearing page number 781, 782, and 783. D64 is a videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like first, since we have a few other tapes, I would just stop before D64 at this very moment, and all the documents referred to by the Registrar are admitted into evidence in part of them the objections have been discussed prior to this final decision. Then we have the videos. You mentioned already D64. Did the parties agree upon which video contained all the elements, is that D64, or should any other videotape be admitted into evidence bearing any additional pieces of video shown to the Chamber? I'm just looking to both parties at this moment. Mr. Stamp, could you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have not been able to agree in respect to the videotapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The videotape presented by the Defence to the Court today and at the conclusion yesterday appears to be the videotape which we served on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I believe it is, if I may, but we have not had an opportunity to go through what was brought today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. What we saw as a matter of fact that there has been an original exhibit listed in the Article 65 ter list. We then had a redacted version only showing those parts which we would need. Then we returned to the full-length version. We then also discussed whether a videotape could be redacted in such a way that it would contain all parts shown to the Chamber, and then as a last development, we had this V000-3822 version. If the D64 videotape would contain every single piece of the videos shown to the Chamber originating from the other tapes, and if you would have been -- have had an opportunity to check that, would then D64 be a sufficient exhibit to be admitted in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It would be. And it would cover the 4th and the 5th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it would cover the 4th and the 5th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would then give you as a decision of the Chamber that the D64 is admitted into evidence under the provision that if the Prosecution, while checking the content of it, would find out that it's not exactly the same but we of course all assume that this is the videotape provided by the Prosecution to the Defence, then of course they then could come back to it and challenge the earlier admission into evidence of this videotape. And then I hope it will never happen, but then we would have to compare the video in the hands of the Registry with the video provided by the Prosecution as it is according to their view. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I think that's indeed the best solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then we have a lot of videos now available to be replayed in the future. That's, Madam Registrar, D64 is then admitted into evidence. Then we have an artifact, which is...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is the -- this bears the Prosecution number P3624.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is now in the hands of the Registry, as soon as it is admitted into evidence. That means that if one of the parties wished --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although it may have been considered before just to mark it for identification, I think especially the way it was used during cross-examination, makes it necessary to give a decision on whether it's admitted into evidence, and it is admitted in evidence. If the Defence expert would like to inspect the artifact, of course, they will be given an opportunity. That should, however, be under the control of the Registry, as you'll understand. And whenever any examination of the artifact is necessary in a way which would damage, if even slightly, we all know that there are techniques of taking out perhaps 1/10th of a gram of material in order to analyse it, then this would need specific approval of the Chamber, and we'll first hear at least the other party on such an examination of this artifact. Having said this, I think we could -- you still are waiting on a decision on when we'll hear the 92 bis. Yes, we have conferred, and it could be done in the beginning of next week. And since Monday might not be the most suitable day to do it, there might be a risk of late arrival or whatever could happen, so perhaps we'll do it Tuesday in the morning. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we'll then hear the parties before giving a decision on the 92 bis request filed by the Prosecution. Is the Prosecution then ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just look on the list. Yes, that would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Ezrema Boskailo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And there is facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Facial distortion as protective measure. Yes, please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I'd like to thank you for the manner in which the Chamber resolved the problem because we would have to come back to it. There is the question of experts, and this question gives rise to another point, and it is simply possible that when Defence experts examine this exhibit, then perhaps other questions will arise, questions which the Defence has not been able to formulate until today. And I hope that it is clear to everybody that the Defence will then perhaps request this witness to be recalled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, what I would expect under these circumstances is that first the Defence then calls its expert while presenting its case, and then from the testimony of this expert, it might become clear that we have to recall the expert or the witness that has been testifying before. And of course the Chamber is always in a position to recall whatever witness they would need to hear again. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank your Chamber for this. But I wanted to avoid in case we are reproached later on in action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. Then, Mr. Usher, could you please bring in Ezrema Boskailo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Boskailo, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving your testimony in this courtroom, the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and the text of this declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. Ms. Boskailo, you'll first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And please be aware that I checked whether your facial distortion is functioning effectively. Yes, Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Stamp:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Ezrema Boskailo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long have you lived there?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: About 30 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You lived there during the conflict in 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you married at the time?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you recall the 5th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That morning, did you leave your home and did you go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you travel alone or did you travel with anyone?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I was with my husband and with my daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many children did you have at that time?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your physical state at that time?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I was pregnant with my third child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the weather like that day?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: The weather, as far as I was concerned, was quite nice. It was a dry day. It was February. It was unusual for that time of the year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall if it was sunny, cloudy, clear?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: It was clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you remain with your husband all that day?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He left you with your daughter?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did yourself and your daughter go anywhere in particular?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: We set off to the market. Because I was pregnant, I wanted to buy something that would cheer me up, because until then I did not have any money and I received some money from my sister. So I wanted to get some cheese and some cream cheese.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should have asked you this before, but what work do you do?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I am a dentist by profession, and I work as a teacher in a secondary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you employed in February 1994?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you attend the market with your daughter?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is the Markale market in the downtown section of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you to tell the Court slowly and in your own words what happened when you went to the market, starting firstly with the approximate time when you arrived at the market with your daughter.

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I can't quite remember the exact time when I arrived there. I know that I left my home about 10.30 in the morning. I stopped in town for a little while, because I wanted to buy shoes for my daughter. In fact, I wanted a shoemaker to make some shoes for her. So we walked. We went towards the market. There was a large crowd there, which was unusual for that time of the year. In fact, during the war, I had never walked with my daughter in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you recall the approximate time you arrived at the market?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Perhaps it was about 11.30, because when I arrived at the market, I walked around a bit. I wanted to buy this cheese and cream cheese, but the seller did not have any change to give me. Next to the market, there is a 22nd of December shop where my friend worked, so I went to see her. And so I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go slowly. You went to the 22nd of December shop to see your friend, but continue slowly.

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I'm sorry. So I stopped by at my friend's. I hadn't seen her for a long time. I left my daughter with her, and I went back to the market.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in the market, did you speak with any of the vendors in the market in particular?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I spoke to the vendor from whom I wanted to buy this cheese and cream cheese.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you buy it?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I have to explain. I came to my friend, I brought the cheese and the cream cheese. But then she said she wanted some, so I returned again to the market. And that vendor was supposed to weigh this cream cheese into two parts. And at that moment, behind my back, I heard a tremendous blast, explosion, and the blast detonation threw me. I was in shock. I did not know what was happening. I did not lose consciousness. As I was thrown by the blast to the side, in fact, I felt myself flying at that moment, and the first thing I thought about was my daughter. I did not know what happened to her. I was in shock. I did not know whether my daughter was alive, what was happening to me. I set off to look for her, to crawl on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you set off -- sorry to interrupt you. When you set off, how did you feel? Were you injured? Did you notice you were injured or not?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I was injured. At first, I didn't realise it. I looked to my right leg. I had short boots on, and I had a coat on. I couldn't see my short boot. My boot was off. A whole part had been torn off, and I also looked down on my left leg, and I had some bleeding. My coat was torn by shrapnel. My leg went dead, maybe from fear. I was worried that I could bleed. But the entire time, I was worried about my child, whether she was alive, where the shell had landed. And then I was four months' pregnant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you started to crawl -- you started to crawl. Towards where?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I started to crawl towards where my daughter was. I wanted to get to her, to see whether she was alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was, you started to crawl towards the 22nd of December building?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now approximately where in the market were you when you heard and felt this explosion which threw you? Were you to the back, to the side, the middle or the front? Can you remember where in the market you were?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. I was somewhere in the middle part of the market.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you started to crawl towards the 22nd of September building, could you see what was happening around you, if anything? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Of course, around me there were many injured people. It is very difficult to explain. There was a man without a leg. A woman, I don't know whether I had -- I was deafened by the blast, but everyone was crying or whimpering, but I wasn't sure that it was that loud, because I think my ears were deafened from the blast. But the more I crawled, the situation was worse. I did not know where to look. Wherever I turned around me, there were lots of body parts. There was a lot of blood. There was lots of everything, the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness, Mr. President, a diagram, a sketch diagram of the accident. I was going to ask her where she was and the direction which she --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is not an exhibit. It is a sketch diagram. I think we had indicated...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you like to tender or just mark it for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Would you please put it on the ELMO, Mr. Usher. Has the Defence received a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd just like to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, even from a distance I can see it. Ms. Boskailo, you can see in front of you on the screen the picture which is on your right-hand side on the ELMO machine. If someone asks you to point at something, then please do it on this machine on your right-hand side, and you'll see that your pointer appears on the screen as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could I, with your leave, Mr. President, ask her to mark it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay, if you want it to be marked then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on that sketch map, there's an area towards the bottom of it with some numbers. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, for the purposes of this illustration, could I ask you to mark in the lines above those numbers the name of the street which was at the front of the market.

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: In front of the market, the front of the market was Tito Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm asking to write, perhaps with a pen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you use the blue pen. Perhaps if possible do it on the ELMO so we can all see it. Mr. Usher, would you please assist the witness. Put it on the machine and use the blue pen, and then write. Yes. Just write the name of the street where the street is.

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Marsal Tito Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you mark on the document with perhaps an X the place where you were approximately when you felt that explosion which threw you.

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would be the stall where you were discussing the apportioning of the cheese.

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you could use dotted -- a dotted line to show us approximately -- we understand the condition you were in -- the direction in which you crawled?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: The blast threw me towards this side, and so I went this way, because I knew there was a passage here towards the 22nd of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the top there where you just pointed to the passage, could you put that last line in the form of an arrow. Where you pointed the passage.

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you crawled to that area, did you realise approximately where the centre of the explosion was?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: At that time, I wasn't thinking about the explosion. I was in a state of great shock. Up to that time, I have lived through shellings. I've seen shellings, and I always thought I would be able to get cover, to hide. But because I wanted to find my daughter and as I was coming across more and more injured people and body parts, I felt that it was indeed a shell that had landed. But I did not go to the 22nd of December because I was stopped. I was prevented from doing so by some people. They tried --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Could I just interrupt you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you're asking for a clarification of the record in the directions, I was about to do the same. Mr. Stamp, for the sake of the record, when the witness testified that the direction she was thrown in by the blast, that was the dotted line going downwards, whereas she testified about crawling to the 22nd of December store, then that's where the dotted line goes upwards again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, and sorry for interrupting you, Ms. Boskailo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were prevented from reaching to the 22nd of December building. What's the correct name of the building? Please help me.

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The building you were crawling to, can you recall the correct name of it?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I don't know the name of the building. I know that the shop, in fact, it's a workshop, a factory, was called 22nd of December, where my friend worked as a secretary in this company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 22nd of December. Thank you. Now, you were stopped by people. What did they do?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: The people approached me to help me, and I was screaming in panic saying that my daughter was around, but they told me that they will take care of my daughter and that they had to take me to the hospital. A man, I don't know who he was, he had a red Golf car. He put three or four of us in his car, and I think we all had suffered slight injuries in comparison to the people who had been left without body parts and who were seriously wounded. So he took us to the hospital. He drove us to the hospital. My daughter stayed at my friend's, and she was screaming, asking for her mother. She did not know whether I was alive at all, and she was in a great state of shock. And so my friend sent her brother to look for me among the dead. And they didn't find me. And my daughter was screaming in panic asking for her mother. And my husband who had left us in the market shortly afterwards, he found out that a shell had landed in Markale. And he thought that he had lost both his wife and his daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you to stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know if it's a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder, I don't know exactly it will be relative short testimony. Let me just confer with the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask the interpreters' booth, since I was just informed that the courtroom will not be needed immediately after we leave it, whether it would be a possibility to go on for -- and I'm also looking for you, Mr. Stamp -- 15 minutes, 20 minutes. Would that be an accurate guess?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That would be accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking it because it's a relatively short testimony, and if we break it up in two parts, that has some disadvantages for all of us, including the witness I would say. But I'm just looking at the booth on what would be possible and what would not be possible.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 15, 20 minutes without the break would be all right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I hear from the booth that some 20 minutes should not create a problem. Unless there's some objection, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I have a plane to catch from Amsterdam. But it does not really matter. The Chamber has all my time at its disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Boskailo we had to discuss -- usually we stop at a quarter to 2.00 -- but we could go on for another 15 or 20 minutes. Everyone is prepared to listen to you. Mr. Stamp, if you can then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That morning, did you see any military activity in the vicinity of the market before that explosion?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of people, what were the character of the people who were in the market that you said were very crowded

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: There were lots of people, it was Saturday. So people as usual. I mean, people shopping, looking for things, walking around, swapping goods and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at the hospital, can you describe what you saw there? Firstly, tell us what hospital you arrived at and briefly describe what you saw at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I was taken to the Kosevo hospital, to the emergency ward. And when that man parked the car and helped me get out of the car, the door of that reception ward, admission ward, was wide open. And there were already very many people there. They were all lying on the floor. And the hospital was milling with people and medical personnel. And there a friend of mine, who recognised me, met me there. I was crying. I was weeping. I was weeping in a panic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain at the hospital that day?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave the hospital eventually?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I left the hospital in the evening. They came to fetch me and took me away, and so I spent the whole day in the hospital. We had to wait to be examined, because there were scores of patients and operations were being performed so that it was only sometime in the evening -- or rather, they came immediately and extended some first aid. But after that, I had to wait for my wound to be treated. And my husband came to fetch me -- rather, they came much before I could leave. My husband and a friend of ours came and took me home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you return to the hospital from time to time for treatment?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes, I had to go to have my wound dressed and treated. It was the first time that I had seen such wounds. Such wounds are very dirty, so the tissue turns necrotic very quickly, and I have to clean the wound every day and dress the wound over and over again. But since I'm of medical profession myself and therefore I knew very many fellow medical doctors and physicians, I also had home care.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get and provide to us copies of a medical report which you obtained from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I have my medical record. I don't know when I handed it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I propose to show her a document marked P226A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Could you assist us, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is a copy of your medical record?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at the top right-hand section of the document, can you see it is dated the 11th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were injured on the 5th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain that, how it is that it is the 11th of February, 1994 on the document?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes, because I did not -- I was not hospitalised. I did not stay in the hospital, and that day when I was in the hospital, you know -- rather, you don't know. I mean, there was panic all around. Everybody was extended aid. Nobody wrote any documents at the time. And the auxiliary personnel, the paramedics and everybody who worked in the hospital were at the ready -- no, not at the ready, they were tending to the wounded so that nobody wrote anything for me nor did they think at that particular moment that it would be important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you returned to the hospital on the 11th of February, 1994, I take it?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Wait -- no, I went to the hospital before that. I went there daily to have my wound dressed, but I never took or asked for any document, for any paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you had known you said of situations and shellings and snipings before.

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said that this was the first time you were injured?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Has this event had any lasting psychological impact on you and on your family?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes. For a long time, I dared not shut my eyes. I could not sleep. No sooner would I close my eyes than a nightmare in my head would start. And the same holds true of my daughter. She was also very distraught, and we are still upset when we think back. My whole family, point of fact, my husband and my other daughter, and my relatives, we were all affected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you personally any lasting physical injury as a result of that event?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I have a scar on my left leg. It is still visible. I have a piece of shrapnel in my left leg, and I have another piece of shrapnel near the mandibular in the lower part of mandible next to my spine. So I am suffering the consequences. I still feel it in my back, in my spine, and my legs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you felt compelled to come here to testify. Can you just tell us briefly why you have come.

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to sleep otherwise. I have a moral obligation towards all the casualties whose bodies perhaps protected me and my unborn baby. And I often think of that. I wake up at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those casualties were the persons who stood between where you were and where the shell exploded?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Let me just confer for one second with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The reason why we took some time to confer is the following: Ms. Boskailo, the Court will not sit tomorrow because of a change in the Court schedule. This would mean for the cross-examination that you would have to stay here in The Hague until next Monday. One of the things I had in mind, whether -- and I really don't know whether it's possible or not, but to find three quarters of an hour somewhere this afternoon. But of course this would need all interpreters there, guards there, transport of General Galic, also Defence because I know that Mr. Piletta-Zanin needs to fly back to his destination. But if, for example, I don't know what was planned, whether Ms. Pilipovic would do it or not. I don't know whether it's possible, but before giving a final instruction as to when we'll resume your examination, that would be the cross-examination by the Defence, I'd like to ask the parties to be available to the Registrar to be informed about whether we could, let's say, perhaps resume at 3.00. If that would not be possible, perhaps then even later. I've also an appointment I have to change this afternoon. But at least not to leave the building immediately, and remain available for the Registry so to know when we will resume, either today or if this would not be possible, then unfortunately you'd have to wait for three days in order to come back Monday morning, 9.30, and then be cross-examined by the Defence. But if we can find a solution to conclude your examination today, we'll do so. If this rather vague situation is acceptable for the parties to finish at this moment, let me just...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I've almost forgotten, Ms. Boskailo, you would have to be available as well. I mean, we cannot continue without you as a witness. But you may have understood that we'll try to do it in order to save you a couple of more days in The Hague just for perhaps less than an hour cross-examination next Monday, so you would be able to return home. So we'll adjourn now, but it's not for sure, until -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, only this: We shall proceed to the cross-examination. I will do it, and I think it will be very brief, and perhaps -- perhaps it might be useful to just go on, perhaps for not more than 15 minutes, so that everybody can be set free within a certain period of time. And to finish it now in one go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, of course, I have to ask the interpreters because I don't want to ask the impossible from the interpreters. You heard what Mr. Piletta-Zanin said, that it might be possible to conclude in -- well, let's say at least in half an hour. It would be a splendid solution, but if you say let's have a break of a quarter an hour first and then take --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We shall do it for the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I thank you from the bottom of my heart for your willingness to do so. If there's no one else who -- I first have to confirm whether the answer of one booth was the combined answer of all booths.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The B/C/S booth confirms, Your Honour. We cannot communicate with the French booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think then that we then, Ms. Boskailo, everyone is ready to hear your answers on the questions of the Defence counsel. First of all, I'd like to thank everyone very much for the spirit shown at this very moment. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, madam. Thank you for being here. And the first question I'd like to ask, I was asked to ask you about the consequences, if there were any consequences of the injury and the incident on your third child.

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: There were no consequences for my third child during the birth. The only thing is, is that I have many consequencing during the pregnancy to actually have to keep it to the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. I will wait for a little while for you to finish your answer for the transcript. Witness, you spoke a minute ago, and this is page 80, line 6, you told us about the shop 22nd of December. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said that this was a factory. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What kind of factory was it?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: It was a factory making clothes, and two-piece suits were made for men and women. I bought suits there for myself, and I also heard that equipment was made there for uniforms, for uniformed persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, madam, do you know if these uniforms were made for the police or for the army or for both?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I believe you. Now, your friend who worked there in that factory, was this factory still operational at the time when your friend worked there?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: She worked there. I had a jacket made for my daughter there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So your friend worked there. So the factory was still operational. Is that how I should understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: No, there was a work obligation, and the people had to go there for work obligation. And in that factory was also -- there was a sale held there, and we were able to buy perhaps a suit for some 20 deutschmark, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to ask Mr. Usher to help us if he can put the sketch on the ELMO, the sketch of the Markale market. Thank you very much in advance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will check whether the sketch is clear on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's very clear. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, madam, you placed on this map certain markings. Now, by chance, if you have to make any others, perhaps the usher could hand you over a black marker, and not the blue marker, as we have to do this to distinguish the markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that right, Mr. President? If that is all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you have a black marker pen. You haven't marked on this map, if you do know, where the impact occurred. If you do know that, could you please mark it.

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I understood this sketch -- I thought that this was the 22nd of December. I believe this was the building, this here. Now, I went --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, I have to interrupt you. Before you're making the markings, we have two problems. One is the repetitiveness of your actions and also the speed of the interpretation. So please could you please wait until I give the instructions to mark.

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, there's nothing to apologise. Thank you very much. Now, madam, you marked on this building which you marked across is the shop of the 22nd of December. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: That's how I understand this sketch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please speak clearly so that we can hear you audibly. Okay, very well. Now, could you please mark next to this cross, could you please mark number 1. Now next to the cross you have placed, could you please mark number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To avoid any misunderstanding, you're referring to the cross made with the black pen, the last one?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you then please add a "1" to the cross, Ms. Boskailo, you just...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely there, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the 22nd of December shop. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which building is it then?

utterances.speaker: EZREMA BOSKAILO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't orient myself very well with this sketch. I know this is where Tito Street is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, madam, please do not mark with that. My instructions, do not use your marker pen unless I ask you to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Boskailo, I'll explain to you why we ask you to wait to mark anything until we explicitly request you to do so. The blue markings are the markings you made on the request of counsel for the Prosecution. The black markings are those you make on an explicit request of the Defence, so therefore if you make a black cross over the blue one, this might confuse us. I think the question was whether you -- and perhaps not use the pen to start with -- whether you could indicate on this map, sketch, exactly where the 22nd of December factory was. Mr. Usher, would you please give the pointer to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is what I was going to ask, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Boskailo, if you first point at things, and only then at a -- at an explicit request, mark them. So the 22nd of December.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
